warmup.q: A payments API runs on a pool of 200 worker threads. Each authorization takes 200 ms, almost all of it waiting on the card issuer. Traffic rises from 800 to 1,500 requests per second. What happens?
options: CPU climbs to 100% and every request gets a little slower
Throughput stops near 1,000 requests per second and latency keeps growing, while CPU stays low
The pool starts more threads to absorb the extra load
Nothing: 200 threads can handle any rate as long as requests are short
warmup.why: Each request holds a thread for 200 ms, so one thread finishes 5 requests per second and 200 threads finish 1,000. The other 500 requests per second wait in the pool's queue, and the queue grows every second. The CPU is idle most of that time, because the threads are blocked, not computing. A fixed pool never grows on its own.

sections.h: A platform thread is an OS thread, and you only get thousands
sections.html:
Before JDK 21, every java.lang.Thread was a thin wrapper around one operating system thread. The JDK now calls these platform threads. The mapping is one to one: new Thread(r).start() asks the kernel for a thread, and the kernel schedules it.

That costs real resources. Each platform thread reserves a stack up front: 1 MB by default on 64-bit Linux (-Xss, or ThreadStackSize in java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal). The kernel commits the pages lazily, but it still keeps the reservation, guard pages and its own bookkeeping per thread. Starting a thread is a system call. Switching between thousands of runnable threads costs the kernel time and costs you CPU caches.

So a JVM is comfortable with hundreds of platform threads, and survives a few thousand. Push to tens of thousands and you start fighting ulimits (the per-user limits the OS puts on processes and threads), memory and the scheduler. A million is out of reach.

Servers have used one style for decades anyway: thread-per-request. Tomcat, the Quarkus worker pool, and every JDBC-based service give each request one thread for its whole life. The code is easy to read. A stack trace tells you the whole story of a request. A debugger steps through it line by line. ThreadLocal context such as the logging MDC or the current transaction just works, because the request never changes threads.

The catch is in the phrase "whole life". The thread stays assigned to the request while the request waits for the database, the fraud service and the card issuer. A blocked thread does no work, but nobody else can use it. You run out of threads long before you run out of CPU.

try.title: Count what a thread costs
steps: Run ThreadCostDemo with the command below. It starts 4,000 platform threads that all stay alive until it releases them, then does the same with 100,000 virtual threads.
Before you look at the output, guess which run finishes first: 4,000 platform threads or 25 times as many virtual threads?
Try -Pargs='5000 1000000' for a million virtual threads. Leave the platform count at 5,000 or less on a laptop.

code.title: ThreadCostDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** * Starts N threads that all block on one latch, so they exist at the same time, * then releases them. First with platform threads, then with virtual threads. * * <p>Args: platform count, virtual count. Default: 4000 100000. * Keep the platform count at 5,000 or below on a laptop. */ public class ThreadCostDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int platform = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4_000; int virtual = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 100_000; time("platform", platform, Thread.ofPlatform()); time("virtual", virtual, Thread.ofVirtual()); } static void time(String kind, int n, Thread.Builder builder) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(n); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { threads.add(builder.start(() -> { try { release.await(); // every thread stays alive until we let go } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } })); } long startedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; release.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); long totalMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-8s %,7d threads alive at once: started in %,5d ms, all finished after %,5d ms (%.1f us per thread)%n", kind, n, startedMs, totalMs, totalMs * 1000.0 / n); } }

alt.title: ThreadCostDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch /** * Starts N threads that all block on one latch, so they exist at the same time, * then releases them. First with platform threads, then with virtual threads. * * Args: platform count, virtual count. Default: 4000 100000. * Keep the platform count at 5,000 or below on a laptop. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val platform = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 4_000 val virtual = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 100_000 startAndRelease("platform", platform, Thread.ofPlatform()) startAndRelease("virtual", virtual, Thread.ofVirtual()) } private fun startAndRelease(kind: String, n: Int, builder: Thread.Builder) { val release = CountDownLatch(1) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = List(n) { builder.start { try { release.await() // every thread stays alive until we let go } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } val startedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 release.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } val totalMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("%-8s %,7d threads alive at once: started in %,5d ms, all finished after %,5d ms (%.1f us per thread)" .format(kind, n, startedMs, totalMs, totalMs * 1000.0 / n)) }

try.expect: Each platform thread costs tens to hundreds of microseconds to start (one busy run here printed about 900 us per thread). Each virtual thread costs a few microseconds, so 100,000 of them finish sooner than 4,000 platform threads. A million virtual threads take a second or two and some heap. Nothing crashes.

sections.h: Little's law tells you how many threads you need
sections.html:
One formula explains the wall. Little's law says that in any stable system:

L = λ × W
requests in flight = arrival rate × time each request spends inside

It holds for supermarkets, call centers and servers, whatever the details. With thread-per-request, every request in flight holds one thread, so L is also the number of threads you need.

Take a payment authorization. It parses the request (2 ms of CPU), calls the fraud service (40 ms), calls the card issuer (120 ms), writes to the ledger (35 ms) and replies (3 ms). That is 200 ms per request, and only 5 ms of it uses a CPU. The figure below shows the shape.

At peak the service gets 1,500 authorizations per second:

L = 1,500/s × 0.2 s = 300 requests in flight = 300 threads

The worker pool has 200 threads. Turn the formula around to get the most it can serve:

λ max = L / W = 200 / 0.2 s = 1,000 requests per second

The other 500 requests per second wait in the pool's queue. The queue grows every second, so latency grows every second, and CPU sits at a few percent. Dashboards show a slow service with idle machines.

Now the issuer has a bad day and its calls take 1,200 ms. W becomes 1.28 s and the same 200 threads cap you at 156 requests per second. A slow dependency shrinks your throughput even though your own code did not change. That is how one slow downstream service takes down a whole thread-per-request fleet.

You have two ways out. Make W smaller, which you often can't, because the issuer is not yours. Or make L cheaper: hold the request somewhere other than an expensive OS thread while it waits.

try.title: Predict the wall, then hit it
steps: WallDemo runs 2,000 fake authorizations that each block for 100 ms, first on a fixed pool of 100 threads. Use Little's law to predict the pool's time before you run it.
Run it with the command below. Ignore the virtual thread line for now.
Predict again for a pool of 200, then run with -Pargs='200 2000 100'. Then try a 300 ms latency: -Pargs='100 2000 300'.

code.title: WallDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l01; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** * Runs N fake "authorize a payment" requests that each block for a while, * first on a fixed pool, then with one virtual thread per request. * * <p>Args: pool size, number of requests, latency in ms. Default: 100 2000 100. */ public class WallDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { int poolSize = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 100; int requests = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 2_000; Duration latency = Duration.ofMillis(args.length > 2 ? Long.parseLong(args[2]) : 100); Runnable authorize = () -> { try { Thread.sleep(latency); // stands in for the card issuer call } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(poolSize)) { for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) pool.execute(authorize); } report("fixed pool of " + poolSize, requests, t0); long t1 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) perTask.execute(authorize); } report("virtual thread per task", requests, t1); } static void report(String label, int requests, long startNanos) { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - startNanos) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-26s %,6d requests in %,6d ms = %,8.0f requests/s%n", label, requests, ms, requests * 1000.0 / Math.max(ms, 1)); } }

alt.title: WallDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l01 import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** * Runs N fake "authorize a payment" requests that each block for a while, * first on a fixed pool, then with one virtual thread per request. * * Args: pool size, number of requests, latency in ms. Default: 100 2000 100. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val poolSize = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 100 val requests = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 2_000 val latency = Duration.ofMillis(args.getOrNull(2)?.toLong() ?: 100) val authorize = Runnable { try { Thread.sleep(latency) // stands in for the card issuer call } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(poolSize).use { pool -> repeat(requests) { pool.execute(authorize) } } // use {} = try-with-resources: close() waits report("fixed pool of $poolSize", requests, t0) val t1 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> repeat(requests) { perTask.execute(authorize) } } report("virtual thread per task", requests, t1) } private fun report(label: String, requests: Int, startNanos: Long) { val ms = (System.nanoTime() - startNanos) / 1_000_000 println("%-26s %,6d requests in %,6d ms = %,8.0f requests/s".format(label, requests, ms, requests * 1000.0 / maxOf(ms, 1))) }

try.expect: 100 threads at 100 ms finish at most 1,000 requests per second, so 2,000 requests take about 2 s (one run here: 2,050 ms). 200 threads halve that to about 1 s. Tripling the latency to 300 ms triples the pool's time to about 6 s. The pool's throughput is threads divided by latency, exactly as the formula says.

refs.title: JEP 444: Virtual Threads (see the Little's law discussion in its motivation)

sections.h: The async workaround, and what it costs
sections.html:
The industry's first answer was to stop holding a thread while waiting. Async code hands the thread back at every wait and continues later on whatever thread is free:

Java
// blocking: one thread per request, held for all 200 ms
Receipt authorize(Payment p) {
    Risk risk = fraud.check(p);              // 40 ms
    Auth auth = issuer.authorize(p, risk);   // 120 ms
    return ledger.record(p, auth);           // 35 ms
}

// async: the thread goes back to the pool at every wait
CompletableFuture<Receipt> authorizeAsync(Payment p) {
    return fraud.checkAsync(p)
        .thenCompose(risk -> issuer.authorizeAsync(p, risk))
        .thenCompose(auth -> ledger.recordAsync(p, auth));
}
Kotlin
// blocking: one thread per request, held for all 200 ms
fun authorize(p: Payment): Receipt {
    val risk = fraud.check(p)                // 40 ms
    val auth = issuer.authorize(p, risk)     // 120 ms
    return ledger.record(p, auth)            // 35 ms
}

// async: the thread goes back to the pool at every wait
fun authorizeAsync(p: Payment): CompletableFuture<Receipt> =
    fraud.checkAsync(p)
        .thenCompose { risk -> issuer.authorizeAsync(p, risk) }
        .thenCompose { auth -> ledger.recordAsync(p, auth) }

CompletableFuture, Reactor's Mono and Flux, Vert.x and Quarkus's reactive stack all work this way. A handful of event-loop threads, about one per core, can keep thousands of requests in flight. It works, and it is why reactive stacks became popular.

You pay for it in the code.

Every library on the request path must be async too. JDBC is blocking, so you need a reactive driver. One blocking call on an event-loop thread stalls every request that shares that loop, and nothing warns you.

The call stack stops meaning anything. When issuer.authorizeAsync fails, the stack trace shows pool worker frames and lambda names, not authorize calling issuer.authorize. A debugger can't step from one stage to the next. A profiler shows time in the event loop.

Control flow turns into operators. A try/catch becomes exceptionally or onErrorResume. A loop with an early exit becomes a recursive chain. ThreadLocal context (the MDC, the security context, the transaction) does not follow the request from thread to thread, so you need a context propagation library.

Kotlin coroutines get closest to the blocking style. A suspend function, which the compiler can pause at a wait and resume later on any thread, reads top to bottom. Coroutines still need suspend-aware libraries, though. A blocking JDBC call inside a coroutine blocks a real thread, and you are back to pool sizing with Dispatchers.IO, the coroutine library's shared pool for blocking calls.

If your code is already reactive and works, keep it. Most payment services are plain blocking code on a pool, and rewriting them as async chains to save threads is a poor trade.

Check yourself: an async service runs on 8 event-loop threads, and someone adds a blocking 50 ms JDBC call to one handler. How many of those requests can the service now serve per second? At most 160. Each loop thread is stuck for the whole 50 ms of every call, so Little's law with L = 8 and W = 0.05 s gives 8 / 0.05 = 160, however fast the CPU is. Every other request on those loops waits behind the blocked calls.

sections.h: Virtual threads: cheap threads, same blocking code
sections.html:
JDK 21 took the other way out: make threads cheap. Virtual threads became a final feature in JDK 21 (JEP 444, the JDK Enhancement Proposal that defines them). A virtual thread is a normal java.lang.Thread, but the JDK schedules it, not the OS. It runs on a small pool of platform threads, about one per core. When it blocks on a socket read, a sleep or a lock, the JDK parks it, saves its stack on the heap, and lets another virtual thread use that platform thread. Lesson 2 of this track shows how.

A virtual thread starts in a few microseconds and needs a small heap object that grows with its stack. A million of them fit on a laptop. So you keep the blocking authorize method and give every request its own virtual thread:

Java
try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (Payment p : incoming) {
        perRequest.submit(() -> authorize(p));   // blocking code, cheap thread
    }
}   // close() waits for every task
Kotlin
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest ->
    for (p in incoming) {
        perRequest.submit(Callable { authorize(p) })   // blocking code, cheap thread
    }
}   // use {} closes the executor, and close() waits for every task

Little's law still holds. At 1,500 requests per second and 200 ms you still have 300 requests in flight. They just don't cost 300 OS threads anymore. If the issuer slows to 1.2 s, you have 1,920 in flight, and that is fine too.

Be clear about what virtual threads do not change:

  • One request is not faster. It still waits 200 ms. Virtual threads give you scale (more requests in flight), not speed.
  • CPU-bound work gains nothing. With 8 cores, at most 8 virtual threads compute at once.
  • Downstream limits stay. Your ledger database pool still has 20 connections. With the thread cap gone, 300 requests reach that pool at once, and the bottleneck moves there. Lessons 3 and 6 of this track deal with it.

The lab makes the wall measurable: the same blocking handler on a fixed pool and on one virtual thread per task.

try.title: Run the same wall on virtual threads
steps: Run WallDemo again and look at the second line this time.
Run -Pargs='100 2000 300'. Predict first: does the virtual thread time triple like the pool's did?
Run -Pargs='100 5000 100'. Predict both lines before you look.
try.expect: The virtual line finishes 2,000 requests in a little over 100 ms (one run here: 165 ms), because all 2,000 sleep at the same time. With 300 ms latency it takes a little over 300 ms: the time follows the latency of one request, not the number of requests. With 5,000 requests the pool needs about 5 s and the virtual run still takes well under a second.

analogy: Picture a restaurant where each waiter is assigned to one table from the moment guests sit down until they pay. While the kitchen cooks, the waiter stands at the table and does nothing. With 20 waiters you serve 20 tables at once, however many seats are empty, and guests queue at the door. Async code is one waiter running between many tables with a notepad of what each table needs next. It works, but the notepad gets complicated. Virtual threads give every table its own waiter, and waiters cost almost nothing to hire. The analogy breaks in one place: the kitchen is still the kitchen. If the slow part is the cooking itself (CPU work) or a pantry with room for only 20 cooks (a connection pool), more waiters don't help.
world: Your Quarkus REST endpoints run on a worker pool with a fixed maximum size (quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads), and Little's law decides when it fills up. A card issuer that slows from 120 ms to 1.2 s during an incident cuts that pool's throughput by about ten times, even though your code didn't change. The same math applies to a Kafka consumer that calls a fraud API per record, and to Temporal activity workers, which run each activity on a thread from a fixed number of slots. When you see latency climbing with CPU at 5%, compute L = λ × W before you add pods.
mistake: The most common mistake is reading "slow and idle" as a CPU or code problem. Latency climbs, throughput flattens, CPU is at 5%, so the team adds pods or raises the pool to 2,000 threads. More threads does lift the cap for a while, but each one reserves 1 MB of stack and adds scheduling work, and the extra requests often just pile up on the database pool instead. Do the arithmetic first: measure W, compute L = λ × W for the peak rate, and compare L with your thread pool and with every pool behind it. Then fix the resource that is actually full.

compare.title: Blocking code that scales: virtual threads vs coroutines

java.title: Java 21+: virtual threads
java.html: // plain blocking code, one cheap virtual thread per payment List<Receipt> authorizeAll(List<Payment> batch) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Receipt>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (Payment p : batch) futures.add(perTask.submit(() -> authorize(p))); List<Receipt> receipts = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Receipt> f : futures) receipts.add(f.get()); return receipts; } } Receipt authorize(Payment p) { Risk risk = fraud.check(p); // ordinary blocking HTTP call Auth auth = issuer.authorize(p, risk); return ledger.record(p, auth); // ordinary JDBC }

kotlin.title: Kotlin: kotlinx.coroutines
kotlin.html: // suspend functions: the compiler turns them into state machines suspend fun authorizeAll(batch: List<Payment>): List<Receipt> = coroutineScope { batch.map { p -> async { authorize(p) } }.awaitAll() } suspend fun authorize(p: Payment): Receipt { val risk = fraud.check(p) // must itself suspend to free the thread val auth = issuer.authorize(p, risk) return ledger.record(p, auth) // blocking JDBC here would block a real thread }

compare.note: Both read top to bottom, and both keep thousands of payments in flight on a few OS threads. The difference is where the magic lives. Kotlin does it in the compiler: only suspend functions can give the thread back, so every waiting call on the path has to be suspend-aware, and a blocking JDBC call needs withContext(Dispatchers.IO), which is a thread pool again. Virtual threads do it in the JDK at run time: any blocking JDK call (sockets, sleep, locks, BlockingQueue) parks the virtual thread, so existing JDBC drivers and HTTP clients work unchanged. You can mix the two: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() runs coroutines on virtual threads, which helps when they call blocking libraries.

worked.title: Size the authorization service with Little's law

steps.say: Write down W for one request, stage by stage. Use p50 numbers from your traces for a first pass, and redo it with p99 for the bad day.
steps.code:
parse        2 ms  (CPU)
fraud       40 ms  (HTTP, waiting)
issuer     120 ms  (HTTP, waiting)
ledger      35 ms  (JDBC, waiting)
reply        3 ms  (CPU)
W          200 ms

steps.say: Compute L at the peak rate. This is how many requests are in flight, so it is how many threads thread-per-request needs.

Compare with the pool you have. 200 threads cap the service at 1,000 requests per second. At 1,500 arriving, the queue grows by 500 every second. After 10 s, 5,000 requests are queued, and a new one waits about 5 s before a thread even picks it up.
steps.code:
λ max = 200 / 0.200 s = 1,000/s
queue growth = 1,500 - 1,000 = 500 per second
wait after 10 s = 5,000 / 1,000/s = 5 s

steps.say: Apply the same law to every resource a request holds, not just threads. The ledger stage holds a database connection for 35 ms. With a pool of 20 connections, that stage alone caps you at 571 requests per second. Fixing the thread pool, with more platform threads or with virtual threads, would only move the queue to the connection pool.
steps.code:
connections needed = 1,500/s × 0.035 s = 53
λ max (ledger)     = 20 / 0.035 s = 571/s   <- the real bottleneck

steps.say: Decide. Raise the connection pool only if the database can take 53 concurrent writes. Then make threads cheap with virtual threads, and keep an explicit limit in front of the issuer and the database. Lesson 3 of this track shows that limit.

lab.title: Measure the wall: fixed pool vs a virtual thread per task
steps: Run the tests once. All five fail with UnsupportedOperationException.
Write LittlesLaw.inFlight (L = λ × W) and LittlesLaw.maxThroughput (λ = L / W). Convert the Duration to seconds as a double first.

Write BlockingRunner.runOnFixedPool: open Executors.newFixedThreadPool(poolSize) in try-with-resources, execute the handler tasks times, and count each finished task in an AtomicInteger. Return the count after the try block.
Run the tests again. The last one takes about 2.5 s: it runs 2,000 tasks of 100 ms on a 100-thread pool, then on virtual threads. Read its assertions to see why the pool can never beat 2 s.
hints: close() on an ExecutorService (JDK 19+) calls shutdown() and then waits for every task. That is why the try-with-resources block makes your method wait.
Count with an AtomicInteger, not an int: the tasks finish on many threads at once. The lesson "Race conditions: why count++ lies" shows what count++ does there.
Duration.toNanos() / 1_000_000_000.0 gives seconds as a double without losing the milliseconds.
lab.done: All five tests in ThreadPerRequestTest pass, two runs in a row.

drill.title: Little's law and the per-task executor, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A Kafka consumer service handles 600 records per second, and each record waits 250 ms on a fraud API. (1) How many records are in flight? (2) A pool of 64 threads processes them: what is the most it can handle per second? (3) Write a method that runs a Runnable once per record, each on its own virtual thread, and returns when all are done.

answer.html: // (1) L = 600/s × 0.25 s = 150 in flight // (2) λ max = 64 / 0.25 s = 256 records per second, far below 600 // (3) static void runAll(List<Runnable> perRecord) { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (Runnable r : perRecord) perTask.execute(r); } // close() waits for all of them }

alt.html: // (1) L = 600/s × 0.25 s = 150 in flight // (2) λ max = 64 / 0.25 s = 256 records per second, far below 600 // (3) fun runAll(perRecord: List<Runnable>) { Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> perRecord.forEach { perTask.execute(it) } } // close() waits for all of them }

recap: A platform thread is one OS thread with a 1 MB stack reserved by default on 64-bit Linux. A JVM handles thousands of them, not millions.
Little's law: requests in flight = arrival rate × latency. With thread-per-request, that is also the number of threads you need.
A blocking service is capped at threads / latency requests per second. A slow dependency lowers that cap while CPU stays idle.
Async and reactive code free the thread while waiting, at the price of async-only libraries, broken stack traces and lost ThreadLocal context.
Virtual threads (final in JDK 21, JEP 444) make threads cheap, so plain blocking code can keep thousands of requests in flight.
They give scale, not speed: one request is no faster, CPU-bound work gains nothing, and downstream pools become the new limit.

explain.prompt: Your manager asks why the payments API tops out at about 1,000 requests per second while CPU sits at 5%. Explain it with Little's law, and say what virtual threads would change and what they would not.
explain.answer: Each authorization takes about 200 ms, and almost all of that is waiting on the fraud service, the issuer and the ledger. With thread-per-request, a request holds a thread the whole time, so 200 threads can finish at most 200 / 0.2 s = 1,000 requests per second. Above that, requests queue for a thread, so latency climbs, while the CPU has almost nothing to do because the threads are blocked. Virtual threads make threads cheap, so we could keep 300 or 3,000 requests in flight without 3,000 OS threads, and the thread cap goes away. They would not make any single request faster, and the next limit would be the database pool and the issuer's own capacity, so we'd need explicit limits there.

deeper.html:
Little's law needs only one assumption: the system is stable, meaning requests leave as fast as they arrive over the long run. It says nothing about the shape of the traffic or the order of service, which is why it works for a payments API as well as for a supermarket.

It does not tell you what happens near the limit. As a pool approaches 100% busy, the queue does not grow smoothly. Short bursts above the average rate make requests wait, and the waits add up faster than the load. A pool that is busy 95% of the time has much longer queues than one at 80%, even though it is only a little busier. That is why capacity planning leaves headroom.

It also explains why thread-per-request held on for so long. If W is 5 ms (an in-memory lookup), 200 threads give you 40,000 requests per second, and nobody needs async code. The wall only appears when W is dominated by waiting on other systems, which describes most microservices. JEP 444's motivation section makes this exact argument: the number of threads limits throughput long before CPU or network do.

One honest question remains: why not shrink -Xss and run 20,000 platform threads? Some teams did. You still pay a system call per thread start, the kernel still schedules 20,000 threads, and too small a stack turns deep call chains into StackOverflowError. A virtual thread's stack lives on the heap and grows only as deep as the code actually goes, so you don't have to guess a size.
